extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical mechanics / hydrostatics (undergraduate/graduate-level readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of core statics principles as applied to liquids and gases (level surfaces, pressure laws, Pascal/Torricelli experiments, Archimedes' principle, and related virtual-displacement reasoning). Intended as textbook material for learning and applying fluid statics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level surfaces (equipressure surfaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of all the points of the liquid at which the same pressure p acts forms a surface — a so-called level surface; the element of the level surface stands at right angles to the direction of the force of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a particle is displaced in the direction of gravity it changes pressure; if displaced at right angles to gravity no alteration of pressure takes place. Example: imagining the earth as fluid and spherical, level surfaces are concentric spheres and radii (directions of gravity) are normal to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure is independent of direction
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure in the interior of a heavy liquid is independent of direction: at a given point the liquid is in a state of equal compression and no force acting on vertical containing surfaces produces a greater compression on one side than the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Pascal's experiments (metal disc supported by liquid pressure, mercury rising in siphon arms, objects held/pushed by surrounding fluid). Use these experiments to show that pressure acts equally in all directions at a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure increases proportionally with depth
rubrics_metrics.description: In a heavy liquid the pressure increases proportionally to the depth below the surface; deeper elements are subjected to greater pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental illustration due to Pascal: effects such as a pierced/closed tube pushing discs, rising mercury in siphons, and objects driven by pressure show the depth-dependence. This yields the linear relation between pressure and depth (used throughout deductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure at base independent of vessel shape
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure at the base of a vessel depends only on the area of the base A, the depth h of the horizontal plane base below the level, and the specific gravity s of the liquid: P = A h s; it is independent of the vessel's form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: as we descend the pressure increases at equal rate whether vessel is narrow or broad; Stevinus's fiction of solidified fluid supplying the place of the walls justifies this. Counterintuitive examples (vessels of equal base-area and pressure-height weighing differently) explained by lateral pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basal pressure as area × depth × specific gravity (P = A h s)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A denotes the area of the base, h the depth of the base below the level, and s the specific gravity of the liquid, then the pressure on the base is P = A h s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both conceptions — imagining whole weight A h s displaced the vertical distance dh or considering weight Adh s descent of centre of gravity — are admissible and equivalent. Used in virtual-displacement arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral pressure law and wedge representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lateral pressure on a vertical wall can be represented by a wedge of liquid; the lateral pressure equals the weight of the wedge (integral of pressure over depth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a cubical vessel of 1 decimetre side filled with water, lateral pressure on a vertical wall equals the weight of the wedge ABCD HI (half a kilogram in example). Use geometric wedges to determine resultant and point of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of application of resultant lateral pressure (centre of gravity of wedge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The point of application of the resultant lateral pressure is the vertical line through the centre of gravity of the corresponding wedge of liquid; for the rectangular wedge construction one finds the point by bisecting KL at M (the vertical through M passes through the wedge's centre of gravity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the wedge resting on the wall, cut off appropriate segments (AX—BL = ½ AC), draw KL and bisect to locate M. This locates the line of action of resultant lateral pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure on inclined base equals AHs (use centroid depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an inclined base divided into elements a, a', a" with depths k, k', k" below liquid level, the pressure on the base is (a k + a' k' + a" k" + ... ) s; if A is total base-area and H the depth of its centre of gravity then pressure = A H s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sum pressures on elements and factor s; shows that the effective depth is the depth of the centroid of the base-area. Practical method to compute basal force on inclined planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of virtual displacements applied to fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of virtual displacements gives clear and comprehensive results in fluid statics: virtual moments of displacements of masses/fluids equate to understand pressure work and forces (used also to derive Archimedes' principle and explain Pascal paradox).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing simultaneous displacements of weights (Fig.71) or lifting a piston (Pascal paradox) leads to equal virtual work whether one conceives whole displaced mass lifted or the weight Adhs lifted dh. Use of virtual moments simplifies paradox resolution and derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal paradox / hydraulic leverage (virtual-work explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vessel with narrow upper and broad lower cylinder closed by a movable piston can balance large weights despite small liquid quantity; explained by virtual displacements and the pressure-height product A h s giving large resultant forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider virtual displacement dh of piston; virtual moment Adh s · h or Ahs · dh — equivalence shows how small fluid mass can produce large balancing force. Variation when liquid is frozen demonstrates role of fluid mobility vs solidified mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' principle (buoyancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body immersed in a fluid is acted on by an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the liquid displaced; the resultant of surface pressures is applied at the centre of gravity of the displaced liquid and is equal and opposite to the weight of that displaced liquid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivations: Stevinus' solidified-fluid thought-experiment and virtual-displacement method both lead to Archimedes' result. Note centres of gravity of body and displaced liquid coincide only for homogeneous solid bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' principle via virtual-displacements (formulaic virtual moment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parallelepipedon of base a, height h and specific gravity q sinking distance dh, virtual moment of transference from upper to lower shaded space is a dh · q h; liquid's moment is a dh · s h; total virtual moment is a h (q - s) dh = (p - q) dh where p is weight of body and q weight of displaced liquid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This virtual-moment accounting yields buoyant force as difference between body weight and displaced-liquid weight; used to show upward excess of pressure equals v·s where v is volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buoyancy unaffected by immersion of containing vessel (locality principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The buoyancy of a body K in liquid A is not affected by immersion of the container of A in another liquid B once K is wholly immersed in A — only the volumes of the body immersed in each fluid subportion contribute proportionally before full immersion in A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual moments: when body partly in B and A, both liquids contribute in proportion to immersed volumes; once wholly in A, further immersion that affects B does not change buoyancy. Use counterfactual reasoning to avoid paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental illustrations of Archimedes (scale experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale experiments with a hollow cube H and a matching solid cube M show that immersing M disturbs equilibrium which is restored by filling H with water — demonstrating the buoyant effect equals weight of displaced fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-experiment variants (hanging vessel of water on independent support etc.) further illustrate the same principle and remove apparent paradox when accounting for surface-pressure equilibrations and level rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: General resultant of normal forces proportional to area×distance is V·x
rubrics_metrics.description: If normal forces act inwards on a closed surface proportional to a·z (a = area element, z = perpendicular distance from a plane E), then the resultant equals V·x where V is enclosed volume; the resultant acts at the centre of gravity of the volume, perpendicular to the plane E and directed toward it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposition follows from considering solidified fluid and is a useful general statement to reduce surface-integrations to volume-integrations; it's a form of applying centroid/first-moment reasoning to pressure distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's theorem instance for curved-surface resultants
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rigid curved surface bounded by a plane curve which encloses area A, the resultant of forces acting on the curved surface is R* = (A Z n_y + (∫/V)2 — A Z V K* cos v) (text gives this specific expression), where Z is distance of surface centroid from plane E and v the normal angle between E and A — a particular case of Green's Theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematically practiced readers will recognize this as a reduction of surface-integrations to volume-integrations (Green's Theorem). Use it to compute resultants on curved surfaces bounded by planar curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygon/triangle of forces proposition (equilibrium by geometric congruence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any three forces acting at a point which are proportional and parallel in direction to the sides of a triangle, and which on meeting by parallel displacement form a congruent triangle, are in equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a form of the parallelogram (and polygon) of forces; deduced by imagining solidified fluid cylinder and reducing to plane-curve normal-force resultants. Generalises to polygons (polygon of forces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of hydrostatic reasoning to gases (aerostatics analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same views that serve in the investigation of liquids apply with slight modifications to gaseous bodies; atmospheric pressure behaves analogously to fluid pressure and can be treated by similar statical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context: Torricelli's and Pascal's experiments showed atmospheric pressure and its variation with altitude; treat air as a fluid column subject to weight, allow barometric determination of height with corrections for density strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torricelli barometer principle (atmospheric pressure measured by mercury column)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sealed tube filled with mercury inverted in a dish leaves a mercury column of about 76 cm — demonstrating atmospheric pressure exerted by a column of air and providing a means to measure atmospheric pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Torricelli replaced water with mercury expecting ≈1/13 length; experiments confirmed ~76 cm column. Use this to deduce atmospheric pressure variation and the concept of a vacuum above the column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's barometer-altitude method and atmospheric pressure analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pascal showed that barometer column height falls at a mountain summit compared to base, enabling determination of mountain height; he established an analogy between liquid pressure phenomena and atmospheric (barometric) phenomena, accounting for adhesion and suction phenomena by atmospheric pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal's experiments include long-tube tests, siphon/mercury comparisons, and the Puy de Dôme measurement. Corrections and multifarious conditions must be considered in practical barometric height determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's modification of Torricelli and siphon demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pascal modified Torricelli's experiment with tubes of different shapes and lengths to exhibit vacua and pressure effects (e.g., abed-shaped tube experiment) and used mercury/water/siphon setups to show atmospheric and liquid pressure equivalence in producing flow and vacua.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: three-armed tube immersed in deep vessel causing mercury to rise and flow; abed-shaped tube showed vacua painful to the finger; these experiments demonstrate pressure-driven phenomena without air-pump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-experimental significance (Guericke and early aerostatics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guericke's experiments (e.g., Magdeburg hemispheres and water-barometer designs) greatly advanced aerostatics and demonstrated atmospheric-pressure phenomena, despite speculative digressions in his writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Guericke's experimental approach and devices as historical examples of early aerostatics; his methods show alternative constructions for barometers and empirical demonstrations of vacuum/pressure effects.
